tagline: A winding mountain road passes a tavern moved seventeen miles
intro: Thomas Jefferson Parkway climbs Carters Mountain just south of Charlottesville, winding toward a summit between Monticello and Montalto. The road continues through curves on its descent to Simeon, then crosses Buck Island Creek near the Rivanna River before entering Fluvanna County. It is numbered SR 53 and provides access to Thomas Jefferson’s Monticello.

The parkway’s state-highway history began with a small section from SR 20 toward Monticello, added to the system as SR 714 in 1930. That section became SR 239 in 1933 and was absorbed into SR 20 in 1941. When SR 20 shifted west in 1947, a short piece of its old route became part of SR 53.

Start the parkway’s eastward climb at SR 20, pass Michie Tavern and reach the Monticello access road, which crosses above the highway. Descending to Simeon brings the junction with James Monroe Parkway, the road south to Monroe’s estate. SR 53 continues past the western edge of Lake Monticello to its end at U.S. 15 in Palmyra.

moments.title: White Hall
moments.text: Stores and taverns supplied a succession of names for the place now called White Hall. Glenn’s Store, William Maupin’s Store, Maupin’s Tavern and Shumate’s Tavern all appear in the community’s naming history. The name White Hall dates to 1835. The earlier names belonged to an election district in northwestern Albemarle County.

moments.title: Our Lady of the Angels Monastery
moments.text: Gouda supports the monastic life at Our Lady of the Angels. Six nuns left Mount Saint Mary’s Abbey in Massachusetts in April 1987 to establish a new Cistercian house. They found a cheese farm with its old machinery intact, but the equipment had been out of use. Neighbors Jim and Margaret Morris taught them cheesemaking, and Gouda production began in November 1990. An expansion completed in February 2008 provided more space and updated equipment. The sisters live a cloistered life of prayer and work. The community follows the Rule of St Benedict through the Cistercian Order of the Strict Observance; manual labor and self-sufficiency are part of that practice.

moments.title: Michie Tavern
moments.text: Michie Tavern reached this part of Albemarle County in pieces. William Michie established it in Earlysville in 1784, providing food, drink and lodging to travelers. After its tavern operation ended between 1830 and 1850, it remained a Michie family home until 1910. Josephine Henderson bought it in 1927 and moved it seventeen miles to a site near Monticello. She wanted a place to display her antiques. The Virginia Historic Landmark now forms part of a collection of historic buildings. A restaurant began here in 1969, and the Meadow Run Mill was moved from Augusta County and reconstructed on the property in 1976.

moments.title: Monticello
moments.text: Mulberry Row preserves traces of the labor behind Monticello: a stone weaver’s cottage, the joinery’s tall chimney and foundations of other buildings. The lane contained workshops and quarters for people Thomas Jefferson enslaved. Enslaved people also maintained the vegetable garden on the slope below it. The Thomas Jefferson Foundation began interviewing descendants of enslaved families in 1993 for the Getting Word oral-history project. An outdoor exhibit opened on Mulberry Row in 2012 to interpret the lives of the people who lived and worked on the plantation. The foundation operates the house and grounds as a museum and educational institution, with Mulberry Row’s remains beside the house Jefferson designed.
moments.notice: Look for the stone weaver’s cottage and the surviving joinery chimney on Mulberry Row.
